g.text: THE SMART STUDY · WELCOME PACK FOR SCHOOLS
Welcome to the SMART Study
Thank you for taking part. This pack explains the study, what it asks of your school and your
families, and the support available to you.
What we're asking of your school
Four things, from September 2027 to September 2028:
Help families get started. Share our welcome message and posters with families in Years
3 to 5, and point anyone with questions to us. [TBC: the school's role in sending out
materials]
Tell us which apps and websites your pupils need for school, such as homework
platforms and your school website, so we can add them to the list that still works on
restricted phones.
Run two short reading and maths assessments in class, in the PIRA and PUMA format:
one in the autumn term 2027 and one in the summer term 2028, about [45] minutes each.
You get your pupils' results.
Tell us how it's going. Three short rounds of feedback, in [December 2027, April 2028
and September 2028]. We'll pay your school [£XX] for each.
Families do the rest, and we support them directly.
The study
The SMART Study has been commissioned by the Department for Education to answer one question:
what is the effect of delaying the acquisition of smartphones for children in Years 3 to 5? Its
findings will inform policy in England and further afield.
schools across England
children in Years 3 to 5
12 months
September 2027 to September 2028
Your school is in the treatment group. Families at your school are being asked to wait for a first
smartphone or, if their child already has one, to set it up with a short list of apps, with guidance and
support from us. Schools in the comparison group carry on as normal. Because schools were allocated
at random, comparing the two groups tells us what difference the approach makes to children's mental
health, sleep and learning.
The study is delivered by IFF Research, PUBLIC and the University of Cambridge.

phone (step by step,
with videos)
Every family uses the same study website. It shows the guide to waiting first, then the set-up guides
for families whose child has a phone, so a family whose child gets a phone during the year already knows
where to go. Nothing is installed on children's phones and nothing is collected from them. The list of
apps and websites was built with parents and children, and families can ask for additions on the study
website or by email. We reply within 5 working days.
Why this study, and why now
Smartphones are arriving earlier. About ten years ago, roughly a quarter of children this age had
their own smartphone. By 2025, around 8 in 10 children aged 10 to 12 did. Much of this is driven by
peers: few families want their child to be the only one without a phone.
Coordination looks promising. A 2026 study by the Institute for Fiscal Studies found that where
at least one in five families at a school pledged to delay smartphones, school-recorded social,
emotional and mental health needs fell by around 8%, with larger falls where uptake was higher. A
randomised trial can test whether that effect is real.
The policy context is moving. From September 2026, all schools by default are mobile phone-free
environments. The government has also announced plans to keep under-16s off social media. The
question of the smartphone itself, and when children should have one, is still open.
Timing. Phone ownership jumps around birthdays, Christmas and the summer holidays. Starting in
September gives families a plan before all three, and a full year to see it through. Working with
children in Years 3 to 5, before most have a phone of their own, puts the focus on waiting rather
than on restricting a phone a child already has.
What your school receives
£500 for taking part, plus [£XX] for each round of feedback.
Your pupils' reading and maths results from both assessments, to use as you wish.
The study website, with the guidance for families in writing and on video, and a school resources
area for you. Only schools and families taking part can sign in.

g.text: You don't need to be the expert. Point them to
the study website or to

from there.

g.text: It happens. Encourage the family to stay in

Data and privacy
We collect nothing from children's phones. The settings families use are built into the phone by Apple
and Google and send nothing to us. The only information we receive is what schools and families choose
to share: feedback rounds, surveys, the two assessments and, for families whose child has a phone,
screenshots of screen time. Families' survey answers are confidential and are not shared with the
school. [Link to privacy notice: TBC]
What to do now
Share our welcome message and posters with families in Years 3 to 5. The posters are on the
school resources page of the study website.
Send us your school's apps and websites at smartphonestudy@public.io.
Book your first assessment session for the autumn term 2027. [TBC: how sessions are
arranged]
Sign in to the study website with the details we've emailed you.
Look out for the first feedback round in [December 2027].
Questions? Email smartphonestudy@public.io. Run by IFF Research, PUBLIC and the University of Cambridge for
the Department for Education.
